metadata.title: A Maximization Technique Occurring in the Statistical Analysis of Probabilistic Functions of Markov Chains
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF→text fallback; .tex source not available (pre-arXiv classic). Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Probabilistic function of a Markov chain
nodes.statement: Let $A=(a_{ij})$ be an $s\times s$ stochastic matrix, $a=(a_i)$ a probability distribution on states, and for each $i$ let $f_i(y)$ be a probability density. The triple $(A,a,f)$ defines a stochastic process $\{Y_t\}$ with density $P(A,a,f)\{Y_1=y_1,\ldots,Y_T=y_T\} = \sum_{i_0,\ldots,i_T=1}^{s} a_{i_0} f_{i_1}(y_1) a_{i_1 i_2} f_{i_2}(y_2)\cdots a_{i_{T-1} i_T} f_{i_T}(y_T)$.
nodes.statement_clean: A hidden Markov model: the observed process Y is a probabilistic function of an underlying Markov chain X with transition matrix A and emission densities f_i.

nodes.name: Likelihood function $P_y(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: Let $\Lambda$ be an open subset of Euclidean $n$-space with smooth assignment $\lambda \to (A(\lambda), a(\lambda), f(\lambda))$. For a fixed sample $y=y_1,\ldots,y_T$, the likelihood is $P_y(\lambda) = P_{y_1\cdots y_T}(\lambda)$ determined from $A(\lambda), a(\lambda), f(\lambda)$ via Eq.\ (1).
nodes.statement_clean: The likelihood as a function of parameter lambda living in an open subset of R^n.

nodes.name: Auxiliary function $Q(\lambda,\lambda')$
nodes.statement: Given $P(\lambda) = \int_X p(x,\lambda)\, d\mu(x)$ on a totally finite measure space, define $Q(\lambda,\lambda') = \int_X p(x,\lambda) \log p(x,\lambda')\, d\mu(x)$.
nodes.statement_clean: The Q-function: expectation under P(lambda) of log p(x, lambda').

nodes.name: Transformation $\mathcal{T}$
nodes.statement: Define $\mathcal{T}:\Lambda\to\Lambda$ by $\mathcal{T}(\lambda) = \{\bar\lambda\in\Lambda \mid \max_{\lambda'\in\Lambda} Q(\lambda,\lambda') = Q(\lambda,\bar\lambda)\}$.
nodes.statement_clean: T maps lambda to the argmax (in lambda') of Q(lambda, lambda').

nodes.name: Fundamental inequality (Theorem 2.1)
nodes.statement: If $Q(\lambda,\bar\lambda) \geq Q(\lambda,\lambda)$ then $P(\bar\lambda) \geq P(\lambda)$. The inequality is strict unless $p(x,\bar\lambda) = p(x,\lambda)$ almost everywhere $d\mu(x)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Increasing the Q-function in its second argument cannot decrease P (Baum's inequality).
assumptions: $X$ is a totally finite measure space with measure $\mu$
$p(x,\lambda)$ is a positive real-valued function on $X\times\Lambda$, measurable and integrable in $x$ for fixed $\lambda$
conclusions: Strict inequality unless $p(x,\bar\lambda) = p(x,\lambda)$ almost everywhere

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: Concavity of $\log t$ and Jensen's inequality applied to the probability measure $dv_\lambda(x) = p(x,\lambda)\, d\mu(x)/P(\lambda)$ yield $\log P(\bar\lambda)/P(\lambda) \geq (P(\lambda))^{-1}[Q(\lambda,\bar\lambda)-Q(\lambda,\lambda)] \geq 0$.

nodes.name: Concavity of $\log$
nodes.statement: Note $d^2/dt^2(\log t) = -t^{-2} < 0$, so $\log t$ is strictly concave for $t>0$.

nodes.name: Apply Jensen's inequality
nodes.statement: Write $\log P(\bar\lambda)/P(\lambda) = \log \int_X [p(x,\bar\lambda)/p(x,\lambda)]\, dv_\lambda(x)$ and apply Jensen on the probability measure $dv_\lambda$ to bring $\log$ inside.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The result is $\log P(\bar\lambda)/P(\lambda) \geq (P(\lambda))^{-1}[Q(\lambda,\bar\lambda)-Q(\lambda,\lambda)] \geq 0$, with strictness unless $p(x,\bar\lambda)/p(x,\lambda)$ is a.e.\ constant.

nodes.name: Critical points and fixed points (Proposition 2.1)
nodes.statement: Let $p(x,\lambda)$ be continuously differentiable in $\lambda$ for almost all $x$. Let $\mathcal{T}:\Lambda\to\Lambda$ be a continuous map such that for each fixed $\lambda$, $\mathcal{T}(\lambda)$ is a critical point of $Q(\lambda,\lambda')$ as a function of $\lambda'$. Then all fixed points of $\mathcal{T}$ are critical points of $P$, and if moreover $P(\mathcal{T}(\lambda)) > P(\lambda)$ unless $\mathcal{T}(\lambda)=\lambda$, all limit points of $\mathcal{T}^n(\lambda_0)$ are fixed points of $\mathcal{T}$ for any $\lambda_0\in\Lambda$.
assumptions: $p(x,\lambda)$ continuously differentiable in $\lambda$ for almost all $x$
conclusions: Fixed points of $\mathcal{T}$ are critical points of $P$
Limit points of $\mathcal{T}^n(\lambda_0)$ are fixed points of $\mathcal{T}$ (under the strict-increase condition)

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement: Since $\partial P/\partial\lambda_i|_\lambda = \partial Q(\lambda,\lambda')/\partial\lambda_i'|_{\lambda'=\lambda}$, $\lambda$ is critical for $P$ iff critical for $Q(\lambda,\cdot)$. Monotonicity of $P$ along the iterates and continuity of $\mathcal{T}$ then force limit points to be fixed points.

nodes.name: Monotone increase under $\mathcal{T}$ (Theorem 3.1)
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions $\Lambda=\mathbb{R}^s$, $\log p_i(x,\lambda_i)$ strictly concave in $\lambda_i$ and tending to $-\infty$, define $\mathcal{T}(\lambda) = \bar\lambda$ where $\bar\lambda_i$ is the unique global maximum of $Q_i(\lambda,\lambda_i')$. Then for all $\lambda\in\Lambda$, $P(\mathcal{T}(\lambda)) \geq P(\lambda)$, with equality iff $\lambda$ is a critical point of $P$ equivalently a fixed point of $\mathcal{T}$.
assumptions: For almost all $x$, $\log p_i(x,\lambda_i)$ is strictly concave in $\lambda_i$ with $\lim_{|\lambda_i|\to\infty} \log p_i(x,\lambda_i) = -\infty$
$Q_i(\lambda,\lambda_i') = \int_X p(x,\lambda)\log p_i(x,\lambda_i')\, d\mu(x)$ has unique global maximizer $\bar\lambda_i$
conclusions: Equality iff $\lambda$ is a critical point of $P$ (equivalently a fixed point of $\mathcal{T}$)

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: $Q(\lambda,\bar\lambda) = \sum_i Q_i(\lambda,\bar\lambda_i) \geq \sum_i Q_i(\lambda,\lambda_i) = Q(\lambda,\lambda)$, so Theorem 2.1 implies $P(\bar\lambda) \geq P(\lambda)$. Strict concavity gives the equality characterization via $\partial Q_i/\partial\lambda_i'|_{\lambda'=\lambda}=0$.

nodes.name: Maximum of $P(\lambda)$ for shifted exponential family (Proposition 3.1)
nodes.statement: If $y_t$, $t=1,\ldots,T$ is a sequence of real numbers and $c_x = c_{x_1}\cdots c_{x_T}$, then $P(\lambda) = \sum_x c_x \prod_{t=1}^T \exp(-|\lambda_{x_t} - y_t|)$ assumes its global maximum at a point $\hat\lambda$ where each $\hat\lambda_i$ is some $y_{t_i}$.
conclusions: $P(\lambda)$ attains its global maximum at $\hat\lambda$ with each component $\hat\lambda_i\in\{y_t\}$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: Compute $\partial Q_i/\partial \lambda_i' = -\sum_t \gamma_t(i)\,\mathrm{sgn}(\lambda_i'-y_t)$ which is monotone decreasing piecewise constant; it changes sign at some $y_t = \bar\lambda_i$, so $Q_i$ is maximized there. Theorem 2.1 then gives $P(\bar\lambda) \geq P(\lambda)$, and as $|\lambda_i|\to\infty$ for any active coordinate $P\to-\infty$, forcing the maximum at such a $\hat\lambda$.

nodes.name: Application to Laplace, Poisson, binomial densities
nodes.statement: Theorem 3.1 applies to (a) the density $f_i(\lambda,y) = c\exp(-k|\lambda_i - y|^\varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon\geq 1$, $k>0$; (b) the Poisson $f_i(\lambda,y) = e^{-\lambda_i}\lambda_i^y/y!$ on non-negative integers; (c) the binomial $f_i(\lambda,y)=\binom{N}{y}\lambda_i^y(1-\lambda_i)^{N-y}$ with $0\leq\lambda_i\leq 1$. The transformation $\mathcal{T}$ is determined by solving $\partial Q_i/\partial\lambda_i'=0$.

nodes.name: Explicit form of $\mathcal{T}(\lambda)$ for the three examples
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{T}(\lambda)_i = \left[\sum_{x\in X}\mu(x)\prod_{t=1}^T v_i(x)\, f_{x_t}(\lambda_{x_t},y_t)\right]\cdot\left[\sum_{x\in X}\mu(x)\prod_{t=1}^T n_i(x)\, f_{x_t}(\lambda_{x_t},y_t)\right]^{-1}$ where $v_i(x)=\sum_{S_{xi}}y_t$ and $n_i(x)$ is the number of elements in $S_{xi}$.

nodes.name: Reestimation in the most important case
nodes.statement: When $\mu(x) = a_{x_1} a_{x_1 x_2}\cdots a_{x_{T-1} x_T}$, $\mathcal{T}(\lambda)_i = \left[\sum_{t=1}^T \gamma_t(i)\, y_t\right]\left[\sum_{t=1}^T \gamma_t(i)\right]^{-1}$, where $\gamma_t(i) = \alpha_t(i)\beta_t(i)$ obtained from forward $\alpha_t(j) = \sum_{i=1}^s \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, a_{ij}\, b_j(\lambda_j,y_t)$ and backward $\beta_t(i) = \sum_{j=1}^s \beta_{t+1}(j)\, a_{ij}\, b_j(\lambda_j,y_{t+1})$ recursions.
nodes.statement_clean: The forward-backward reestimation formula for emission parameters in an HMM (the heart of what is now called the Baum-Welch algorithm).

nodes.name: Gamma density
nodes.statement: For $f_{\alpha,v}(r) = \Gamma(v)^{-1}\alpha^v r^{v-1} e^{-\alpha r}$, $\alpha>0$, $v>0$, the Hessian of $Q_i$ in $(\alpha_i',v_i')$ is negative definite (using the infinite expansion of $\log\Gamma(v)$), so $Q_i$ has a unique critical point which is the global maximum and Theorem 3.1 applies though no closed-form $\mathcal{T}$ exists.

nodes.name: Cauchy density counterexample
nodes.statement: For the Cauchy density $f(r) = \pi^{-1}(1+r^2)^{-1}$, $d^2 f/dr^2 = -2\pi^{-1}(1-3r^2)(1+r^2)^{-3}$ is concave only for $3r^2\leq 1$, so $\partial Q_i/\partial\lambda_i' = (2/\pi)\sum_{t=1}^T \gamma_t(i)(y_t-\lambda_i')/(1+(y_t-\lambda_i')^2)$ need not have a unique zero; further procedure is needed to pick the global maximum.

nodes.name: Location-scale generalization (Theorem 4.1)
nodes.statement: For $i=1,\ldots,s$ let $f_i(u)$ be a strictly log concave density with unique local maximum at $u=0$, and assume the non-pathology condition: there exist times $t_n=t_n(i)$, $n=1,2$ with $y_{t_1}\neq y_{t_2}$ and $\sum_{x:x_{t_n}=i} v_x(m,\sigma) > 0$, $n=1,2$. Then for fixed $m$ and $\sigma$, the system $\partial Q/\partial m_i'=0$, $\partial Q/\partial\sigma_i'=0$ has a unique solution $\{\bar m_i', \bar\sigma_i'\}$ which is the global maximum of $Q(m,\sigma,m',\sigma')$. Defining $\mathcal{T}(m,\sigma) = \{\bar m_i', \bar\sigma_i'\}$ we then have $P(\mathcal{T}(m,\sigma)) \geq P(m,\sigma)$ with strict inequality unless $(m,\sigma)$ is a critical point of $P$, equivalently $\mathcal{T}(m,\sigma)=(m,\sigma)$.
assumptions: Each $f_i(u)$ strictly log concave with unique local maximum at $0$
conclusions: Unique global maximizer $\{\bar m_i', \bar\sigma_i'\}$ of $Q$ exists
$P(\mathcal{T}(m,\sigma)) \geq P(m,\sigma)$ with strict inequality off fixed points

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: Show $Q(m,\sigma)\to-\infty$ as $(m,\sigma)\to\partial\Omega$ and $Q$ has a unique critical point in $\Omega$ that is a local hence global maximum, then apply Theorem 2.1.

nodes.name: Boundary behavior of $Q$
nodes.statement: Show $Q(m,\sigma)\to-\infty$ as $(m,\sigma)$ approaches the boundary $\partial\Omega$ using $e^{-a|u|} < a^{-1}|u|^{-1}$ for small $a$, large $|u|$, and the non-pathology condition guaranteeing a $t=t(m)$ with $z_t\neq 0$ and $\gamma_t > 0$.

nodes.name: Critical points are local maxima
nodes.statement: Compute the Hessian of $Q(m,\sigma)$ at a critical point and show $\sigma^4 \det(H) > 0$ together with $\partial^2 Q/\partial m^2 < 0$, so $H$ is negative definite at any critical point. Topology (Morse theory) then gives a unique critical point that is a global maximum.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 2.1
nodes.statement: Since $Q(m,\sigma,\bar m',\bar\sigma') \geq Q(m,\sigma,m,\sigma)$ (the maximizer is unique), Theorem 2.1 gives $P(\mathcal{T}(m,\sigma)) \geq P(m,\sigma)$ with the strict-inequality characterization.

nodes.name: Closed-form reestimation for the normal case (Corollary 4.1)
nodes.statement: Let $f(u) = \exp(-c|u|^\alpha)$ with $\alpha>1$. Then $\log f(u) = -c|u|^\alpha$ is strictly concave so Theorem 4.1 applies. For $\alpha=2$ (the normal distribution) the unique critical point is $\bar m_i = [\sum_t \gamma_t(i)\, y_t][\sum_t \gamma_t(i)]^{-1}$, $\bar\sigma_i^2 = [\sum_t \gamma_t(i)\, y_t^2][\sum_t \gamma_t(i)]^{-1} - \bar m_i^2$.
nodes.statement_clean: For Gaussian emissions, the M-step gives the standard weighted-mean and weighted-variance reestimation formulas.

nodes.name: Reestimation of stochastic matrix and initial probabilities
nodes.statement: $\bar a_i' = [\sum_{x_0=i} p(x,a,A,f)][\sum_x p(x,a,A,f)]^{-1}$, $\bar A_{ij}' = [\sum_x p(x,a,A,f)\sum_{x_{t-1}=i,x_t=j}1][\sum_x p(x,a,A,f)\sum_{x_{t-1}=i,t\geq 1}1]^{-1}$, $\bar f_j'(k) = [\sum_x p(x,a,A,f)\sum_{x_t=j,y_t=k}1][\sum_x p(x,a,A,f)\sum_{x_t=j}1]^{-1}$. The transformation $\mathcal{T}:\{a,A,f\}\to\{\bar a,\bar A,\bar f\}$ increases $P(a,A,f)$.
nodes.statement_clean: The full Baum-Welch reestimation formulas for HMM parameters (initial distribution, transition matrix, emission distribution).

nodes.name: Growth transformation $\mathcal{T}$ (Baum-Welch reestimation)
nodes.statement: Iterative procedure: starting from $\lambda_0$, iterate $\lambda_{n+1} = \mathcal{T}(\lambda_n)$ where $\mathcal{T}(\lambda) = \arg\max_{\lambda'} Q(\lambda,\lambda')$. Each step is guaranteed to non-decrease the likelihood $P(\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_clean: The growth transformation iterative algorithm for maximum-likelihood estimation of HMM parameters; precursor of the EM algorithm.
input: Initial parameter $\lambda_0 \in \Lambda$ (initial distribution $a$, transition matrix $A$, emission densities $f$)
output: Limit points are critical points of the likelihood $P$

nodes.name: Initialize
nodes.statement: Choose initial parameter $\lambda_0 = (a^{(0)}, A^{(0)}, f^{(0)}) \in \Lambda$.

nodes.name: Forward-backward computation of $\gamma_t(i)$
nodes.statement: Compute $\alpha_t(j) = \sum_{i=1}^s \alpha_{t-1}(i)\, a_{ij}\, b_j(\lambda_j,y_t)$ forward and $\beta_t(i) = \sum_{j=1}^s \beta_{t+1}(j)\, a_{ij}\, b_j(\lambda_j,y_{t+1})$ backward. Set $\gamma_t(i) = \alpha_t(i)\beta_t(i)$, the likelihood of the event $\{Y_1=y_1,\ldots,Y_T=y_T,X_t=i\}$.

nodes.name: Reestimate parameters
nodes.statement: Update $\lambda_{n+1} = \mathcal{T}(\lambda_n)$ via the explicit formulas: $\bar a_i' = \gamma_1(i)/\sum_i\gamma_1(i)$; $\bar A_{ij}'$ ratios of $\sum_t \xi_t(i,j)$ over $\sum_t \gamma_t(i)$; $\bar f$ from the emission-specific formula (e.g. weighted mean for Gaussian via Cor.\ 4.1).

nodes.name: Iterate until fixed point
nodes.statement: Repeat steps 2--3. By Theorem 2.1, $P(\lambda_{n+1}) \geq P(\lambda_n)$. By Proposition 2.1, all limit points of $\{\lambda_n\}$ are fixed points of $\mathcal{T}$, hence critical points of $P$.

nodes.name: Maximum-likelihood estimation for probabilistic functions of Markov chains
nodes.statement: Given a fixed $Y$-sample $y = y_1,\ldots,y_T$, find a parameter value $\lambda^0 = \arg\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda} P_y(\lambda)$, where $P_y(\lambda) = P_{y_1\cdots y_T}(\lambda)$ is determined from $A(\lambda), a(\lambda), f(\lambda)$ via Eq.\ (1).
nodes.statement_clean: Maximum-likelihood estimation for hidden Markov model parameters.
